{"id": "1:5/q05", "question": "What does نَعْبُدُ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether worship is fundamentally submission, obedience, affirming unity, supplication, or devoted service", "positions": [{"id": "1:5/q05/p1", "position": "Worship fundamentally means humility and submission.", "reasons": "KASHSHAF (author): Worship is utmost submission and abasement; related ʿabada describes thick, strongly woven cloth. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Worship is the utmost submission and humility, reserved for God because He is the giver of the greatest blessings. IBNATIYYA (author): The believer's declaration confesses God's lordship, expresses humility, and affirms worship of God, unlike people who worship idols. IBNATIYYA (author): Naʿbudu means to uphold the law and commands with humility and submission; maʿbad likewise names a smoothed path or camel. IBNATIYYA (طرفة): Ṭarafa's phrase “over a smoothed path” supports the lexical sense of maʿbad as something made smooth. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Worship means observing the law and commands with humility and submission; maʿbad describes a well-trodden path or a tamed camel, as in Tarafa's line. TABRISI (author): Worship linguistically means abasement, as in a road worn smooth by traffic or a camel coated with tar; seeking assistance means asking for help. RAZI-FULL (author): Razi moves from lordship to servitude: the body is an instrument for the soul, and worship is its best state and the first stage of human felicity; divine aid and guidance are the next stages. RAZI-FULL (author): Worship is an act performed to magnify another; the word is related to a well-trodden, level road, طريق معبد. RAZI-FULL (author): Because an individual's worship is mixed with shortcomings, he joins it to the worship of all worshipers; like a sale of ten slaves accepted all together or rejected all together, God may accept it with the worship of angels, prophets, and saints. RAZI-FULL (author): Worship is a trust: fulfilling it is required and intrinsically excellent, and faithfulness in one direction brings God's faithfulness in return; 33:72 and 4:58 support the duty. RAZI-FULL (أهل التحقيق): The highest rank worships God because He is God and Creator and the worshiper is His servant; this joins awe with humility, and intending prayer for God keeps it valid. QURTUBI (الهروي): Naʿbud means we obey; worship is obedience joined with humility. Al-Harawī compares a trodden, smoothed road called muʿabbad. BAYDAWI (author): ʿIbāda is utmost submission and humility, from maʿbad, a smoothed road, and a garment of exceptional thickness; thus it is used only for submission to God. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): ʿIbāda is the utmost submission and abasement, and is used only for submission to God. ABUHAYYAN (الجمهور): The majority explain worship as humility and submission, which Abū Ḥayyān later identifies as the basic lexical sense. ABUHAYYAN (author): Worship is an exalted station, commanded in scripture and used as an honorific for the most excellent creatures, including the Prophet and Jesus. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن السكيت): Ibn al-Sikkīt glosses ʿibāda as tajrīd, while the majority gloss it as humility and submission. SAMIN-DURR (author): Worship is ultimate submission, due only to the ultimate benefactor, and is stronger than ʿubūdiyya, which is outwardly showing submission. IBNKATHIR (بعض الصوفية): Some Sufis criticize worship motivated by reward or avoidance of punishment, and even worship as honor through religious duties, arguing that the highest worship is for God's own perfection. BIQAI (الحرالي): Al-Ḥarālī defines worship as reaching the utmost degree in all forms of humble submission. BIQAI-FULL (author): Worship is possible only through God's aid, and guidance lies in His hand; the sequence moves from essence to acts to attributes and back to essence, teaching dependence after recognizing God's right. DURR-FULL (ربكم): The continuation of Ubayy b. Kaʿb's report assigns the first three Fātiḥa verses to God, the middle verse to both, and the final three to the servant; worship is the servant's and aid comes from God. BURSEVI (author): Pairing worship with dependence combines pride in serving God with humility about needing His aid, and removes worshipper's conceit. ALUSI (author): Worship is the highest degree of submissive humility. ALUSI (قيل): Some restrict the word worship to submission directed to God; references to people worshipping other things describe their own false assumption and rebuke their stupidity. ALUSI (بعض المحققين): Some careful scholars distinguish three levels: worship for reward or fear of punishment (the lower level, called ʿibāda); worship as honor, acceptance of duties, or affiliation (the middle level, ʿubūdiyya); and submission solely because God deserves it (the highest, ʿubūda). ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī’s note says his three-level account answers the objection that, if worship is the highest submission, most believers would not count as worshippers. ALUSI (author): For the gnostic, God is the first and primary object of attention; worship is only a vehicle of approach, leaving the seeker absorbed in divine majesty and beauty. ALUSI (author): Since worship is a trust, al-Ālūsī says concern for fulfilling it warrants placing it first. ALUSI (author): Worship is a means, so placing it before the request for aid is like offering a means before asking for what one needs. ALUSI (author): Worship is an inescapable duty and is presented as the purpose for which humans and jinn were created, so it has priority. ALUSI-FULL (author): Worship is the highest degree of submission and is due only to God, who bestowed the greatest gifts of life and existence; therefore prostration to another is forbidden. ALUSI-FULL (author): Worship is a means, so it properly precedes the request for a need and may make that request more readily answered. ALUSI-FULL (author): Worship is an unavoidable duty and the stated purpose for creating humans and jinn, so it deserves precedence. ELMALILI (author): True worship unites outward and inward submission without pride or ostentation; arrogant people, heedless optimists, and despairing pessimists are excluded from its honor. ELMALILI (author): The proud objector asks whether worship's humility is degrading for a soul that wants to rise or believes it has already risen. ELMALILI (author): Although humans have no inherent rights before God, He recognizes their rights and assumes them under His mercy; worship is His right and the servant's duty, while aid, reward, and punishment become human claims by His own commitment. ELMALILI (cumhûr-i müfessirîn): The majority of exegetes define worship as the utmost degree of humility, which entails complete obedience without asking the reason. ELMALILI (author): Another explanation says worship is doing what God approves while ubudiyet is being content with what God does; its usage can be narrower or broader, and Prophetic ubudiyet is more specific than ibadat. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ordinary العبادة is submissive or exceptionally reverent action; obedience is a figurative extension. In religious usage it is whatever pleases God through submission, compliance, and avoidance, including all law. IBNASHUR-FULL (الرازي): Al-Razi says worship means honoring God's commands and caring for creation, the shared purpose of revealed laws despite their differing forms and details. TABATABAI (author): A servant is a human or any conscious being in a state of ownership; worship is setting oneself in the position of one's Lord's possession. TABATABAI (author): Worship differs from mere humility in grammar and meaning: the lexicographer's account of servitude as submission captures an implication, since worship takes a direct object while submission takes li. TABATABAI (author): Worship is incompatible with arrogance but can be shared, as shown by the prohibition on associating another in worship; arrogance, by contrast, cannot coexist with worship. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT (روح المعاني): Since worship is unavoidably obligatory for servants, it is more deserving of precedence than seeking aid. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT (التفسير القيم): Putting worship before seeking aid follows the rule that ends precede means: worship is the end and aid its instrument. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT (author): Worship is God’s due, whereas seeking aid is the servant’s request; offering submission first is fitting before asking for something. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT (روح المعاني): Worship is more apt beside the mention of recompense, and seeking aid joins more closely to the request for guidance. STUDYQURAN (author): Some define true servitude as maximal humility and self-effacement; it acknowledges human poverty and reliance on God (47:38)."}, {"id": "1:5/q05/p2", "position": "Worship means affirming God's oneness.", "reasons": "IBNJAWZI-ZAD (علي وابن عباس في آخرين): One interpretation of worship is affirming God's oneness, reported from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās among others. RAZI-FULL (author): The familiar remembrance combines glorification, praise, monotheism, divine greatness, and dependence; “praise belongs to God” already entails glorifying Him because only the perfect can perfect others. RAZI-FULL (author): Naming God before the act prevents the devil from claiming the worship was directed to idols, celestial bodies, or another object; the order makes monotheism explicit. RAZI-FULL (author): After establishing God's oneness, God commands Moses to worship Him: monotheism is the root or tree, and servitude its branch or fruit; neither stands without the other. ABUHAYYAN (author): Worship is also explained as affirming God's oneness, as in the statement that jinn and humankind were created only to worship. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Worship is a noble station: scripture applies servant to prophets and places worship after monotheism, since worship follows the foundation of divine unity. BURHAN (القاضي أبو بكر بن العربي): Ibn al-ʿArabī groups the Qurʾān’s core subjects into monotheism, reminder—i

BIQAI-FULL (author): Al-Baqara is also called the Radiant and the Hump: it illuminates guidance and sufficiency, brightens believers' faces at judgment, and exalts belief in the afterlife above every other good after monotheism. DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas glosses worship as affirming God's oneness, fearing and hoping in Him as Lord, and worshipping no other. BURSEVI (عكرمة): Ikrima says worship wherever used in the Qur'an means monotheism, tasbih means prayer, and qunut means obedience. ALUSI (author): Worship may mean affirming divine oneness, as in the stated purpose for creating jinn and humankind. ALUSI-FULL (author): The early explicit focus on God strengthens monotheism and guards against distraction, satanic whispering, and the thought that worship might be meant for someone else. ELMALILI (author): The verse is pure monotheism and rejects every form of associating partners with God. MUQATIL (author or reported authority): Worship affirms God's oneness; the servant asks help for worship, and a report divides the sūra between God and the servant."}, {"id": "1:5/q05/p3", "position": "Worship includes love or reverence with submission.", "reasons": "TABRISI (author): Worship is the highest gratitude: utmost submission joined with utmost reverence, owed only to God as giver of life's foundational blessings. RAZI (author): Worship is performing an act that has been commanded, out of reverence for the commander. RAZI-FULL (author): Worship is performing an act commanded by the one obeyed, out of reverence for that commander. IBNKATHIR (author): In ordinary language ʿibādah is rooted in humility, as in a subdued road or camel; in religious usage it combines complete love, submission, and fear. ALUSI (قيل): Since worship is harder than praise, placing it in the language of presence helps the lover perform it energetically and without weariness; a poem pictures the beloved seeing and hearing. ALUSI-FULL (author): Because worship is demanding, the beloved's presence gives the servant energy to endure hardship without fatigue, as illustrated by a poetic appeal to sing before Saʿdā. ELMALILI (author): Worship is obedient action born from the collision of supreme love and fear, seeking ascent from total helplessness to absolute power and seeking tranquility through ultimate humility and reverence. ELMALILI (author): Humility and reverence toward God provide the highest possible elevation for the human conscience through affiliation with Him. ELMALILI (author): Narrowness of conscience accompanies ignorance and pride, while an expanded conscience accompanies elevated understanding, humility, mercy, patience, and forbearance; the narrow-hearted person loves and fears only himself. ELMALILI (author): Ubudet is the broadest term, while ibadat is narrower; ubudiyet displays humility and ibadat expresses its strongest form, including awe and reverence. IBNASHUR (author): Worship ordinarily denotes an act of submission or reverence exceeding what is customary between people; using it for obedience alone is metaphorical. IBNASHUR (author): In religious usage worship is doing what pleases the Lord through submission, compliance, and avoidance, or a morally accountable person’s action against personal desire in reverence for God. IBNASHUR (author): Worship is driven by reverence, either from love or bare fear; love is more important because it pleases the worshipper, and it entails fearing the beloved’s displeasure. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Worship combines love, fear, and submission; it is humanity’s purpose but remains a free choice under life’s test, and worldly gifts are means for serving God rather than ends."}, {"id": "1:5/q05/p4", "position": "Worship can mean supplication.", "reasons": "IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): A third meaning is supplication, as in the warning about those too proud to worship God in Ghāfir 40:60. ABUHAYYAN (author): Worship is also interpreted as supplication, as in the warning against those who disdain worship. ABUHAYYAN (author): The meanings offered for worship—humility, obedience, drawing near, supplication, and affirming oneness—are close in sense. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الجمهور): Most interpret worship as submission and humility; other contextual senses include obedience, drawing near through obedience, supplication, and affirmation of divine unity. BIQAI-FULL (author): The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly. ITQAN (author): The worshippers speak this supplication; an implied “say” can be supplied, as with the two earlier human utterances, unlike Gabriel’s and the angels’ speech. ITQAN (author): Declarative form can express supplication: ask for help, curse Abu Lahab, or invoke ruin and a curse on others. ALUSI (author): Worship can also mean supplication, as in the warning against those who are too proud to worship God. ALUSI (author): These senses of worship—submission, obedience, supplication, and affirming oneness—are close in meaning. ALUSI-FULL (author): Names nine through thirteen include al-Hamd, al-Shukr, al-Duʿa, Taʿlim al-Masʾala, and al-Suʾal, reflecting praise, gratitude, supplication, and asking. ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi finds the claim that the surah contains supplication or asking more difficult than the claim about gratitude; it begins with praise before the request. ALUSI-FULL (author): Worship may mean submission, obedience, supplication, or affirming God's oneness; the meanings are close, and references to worshipping idols report the opponents' claim sarcastically. ALUSI-FULL (author): A structural explanation takes the first part as praise, naturally spoken about God, and the remainder as supplication, naturally spoken in His presence. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author or reported authority): Worship is exclusive humble obedience and help is sought from God."}, {"id": "1:5/q05/p11", "position": "The rejected view is challenged: worship fundamentally means humility and submission.", "reasons": "ELMALILI (author): Claiming to have risen already falsely treats progress as finite and decline as impossible; ascent is limitless and the danger of falling remains, so worship is pride's remedy."}, {"id": "1:5/q05/p12", "position": "Worship is humble obedience; the repeated object may add emphasis or satisfy each verb; wāw need not show sequence.", "reasons": "WAHIDI-BASIT (author or reported authority): Worship is humble obedience; the repeated object may add emphasis or satisfy each verb; wāw need not show sequence."}, {"id": "1:5/q05/p13", "position": "Worship is obedience with submission, and aid is sought from God.", "reasons": "WAHIDI-QT (author or reported authority): Worship is obedience with submission, and aid is sought from God."}]}
{"id": "1:5/q06", "question": "How is نَعْبُدُ read and parsed?", "turns_on": "The form of the verb, including person, voice, prefix and final consonant", "positions": [{"id": "1:5/q06/p1", "position": "The initial nūn is read with kasra.", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL (الأعمش وابن وثاب والنخعي): Al-Aʿmash, Ibn Waththab, and al-Nakhaʿi read نستعين with kasra on its initial nūn, a dialect of some Quraysh in certain augmented verbs. ABUHAYYAN (أبو جعفر الطوسي): Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭūsī identifies the kasra on the initial nūn as the dialect of Hudhayl. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (عبيد بن عمير الليثي، وزر بن حبيش، ويحيى بن وثاب، والنخعي، والأعمش): These readers use kasra on the nūn, a dialect attributed to Qays, Tamīm, Asad, and Rabīʿa; al-Ṭūsī attributes it to Hudhayl. ALUSI (بعضهم): Some also read yaʿlamūn with a kasra on the imperfect prefix. ALUSI-FULL (عبيد بن عمير الليثي وزيد بن حبيش ويحيى بن وثاب والنخعي): They read naʿbudu with kasra on the initial nūn, a dialect found among Qays, Tamim, Asad, Rabīʿa, and Hudhayl; the same pattern applies to nastaʿīn."}, {"id": "1:5/q06/p2", "position": "A third-person passive form is reported.", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN (author): The passive reading iyyāka yuʿbadu seems to lack a governor for the accusative pronoun; Abū Ḥayyān explains it as a metaphorical substitution of nominative anta, followed by an unusual shift to third person. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The passive reading iyyāka yuʿbadu is grammatically difficult because iyyāka is accusative; Abū Ḥayyān explains it through metaphorical pronoun substitution and an internal shift. ALUSI (الحسن وابن المتوكل وأبو محلف): Al-Ḥasan, Ibn al-Mutawakkil, and Abū Miḥlaf read yuʿbadu in the passive; al-Ālūsī calls this unusual. ALUSI-FULL (الحسن وإبن المتوكل وأبو محلف): They read yuʿbadu in the passive, an unusual form."}, {"id": "1:5/q06/p3", "position": "The familiar active form is read.", "reasons": "DURR (علي): Abu Razin says Ali read the worship and help clauses, followed by ihdina, in the raised form; he characterizes Ali as a fluent Qurayshi Arab. ALUSI (الجمهور): The majority read naʿbudu with an open nūn and a ḍamma on the dāl; al-Ālūsī identifies this as the eloquent Hijazi form."}, {"id": "1:5/q06/p4", "position": "The final dāl is read without a vowel.", "reasons": "ALUSI (بعض أهل مكة): Some people of Mecca read naʿbud with a quiescent dāl."}]}
{"id": "1:5/q07", "question": "What does worship require and why is it owed to God?", "turns_on": "The grounds, scope, and conditions of worship in the notes", "positions": [{"id": "1:5/q07/p1", "position": "Worship embraces commanded acts and is owed to God for His lordship and gifts.", "reasons": "TABRISI (author): The prayer seeks help for future worship, and asking remains fitting under obligation because the servant shows dependence; prayer may also be needed before God grants a further grace. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): A second meaning is obedience, as in the command not to worship Satan in Yā Sīn 36:60. RAZI (author): Worship requires proving that the world has one God, able to do all possible things, knowing all knowable things, and free of need; He commands and forbids, so creatures must obey and submit. RAZI (author): The obligations encompassed by worship also include those God revealed through earlier prophets and those He assigned to the angels in heaven from their creation. RAZI-FULL (author): Worship and seeking aid concern carrying out the whole range of religious obligations. RAZI-FULL (author): The law, path, and reality complete human ascent: worship, reliance on God, and guidance culminate in fellowship with the pure and distance from the wretched. RAZI-FULL (author): Worship presupposes proof that the world has one God, with unlimited power and knowledge and no needs, who commands and forbids and must be obeyed. RAZI-FULL (author): God alone deserves worship because ultimate reverence belongs only to the source of greatest benefaction: life and the creation of what sustains life, both traced to God. RAZI-FULL (author): Everything contingent is needy and occupied with its own needs, so only the self-sufficient God can meet the needs of others and deserves their worship. RAZI-FULL (author): Calling Muhammad God's servant at the supreme Ascension shows servitude's honor; some say it exceeds prophethood because it turns from creation to God, while prophethood turns back to people and their affairs. RAZI-FULL (author): Jesus first calls himself God's servant; that declaration vindicates his mother, brings good and averts harm, and precedes God's raising him, so sustained practical servitude deserves hope of Paradise. RAZI-FULL (author): Calling the Fatiha “prayer” shows that religious law serves human interests: people most need knowledge of God's lordship and servitude, which the surah's two halves provide to fulfill the covenant. ABUHAYYAN (author): Worship can also mean obedience, as in the command not to worship Satan. ABUHAYYAN (author): Some interpret worship here as drawing near to God through obedience. SAMIN-DURR (author): Neither verb names an object, allowing the wording to encompass every object of worship or aid, or to focus on performing the acts without regard to an object. IBNKATHIR (قتادة): Qatadah says God commands His servants to devote worship sincerely to Him and seek His help for their affairs. IBNKATHIR (بعضهم): Some argue that servanthood is nobler than messengerhood because worship proceeds from creation to God, while the messenger's mission proceeds from God to creation; Ibn Kathir rejects the claim and its reasoning. IBNKATHIR (author): Worship and reliance recur together elsewhere in the Qur'an, including commands to worship God and trust Him. BIQAI-FULL (مسعود التفتازاني): Al-Taftazani maps the Fatiha's blessings to two creations and two preservations: creation in Rabb al-alamin, preservation in mercy, second creation in judgment, and afterlife preservation in worship onward. ITQAN (author): The Fatiha points to all major Qur’anic disciplines: knowledge of God and attributes, prophecy, resurrection, worship, ethical conduct and the straight path, and stories teaching the outcomes of obedience and disobedience. ITQAN (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari says the Fatiha encompasses praise, worship through commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; every Qur’anic verse falls under one of these topics. ITQAN (ابن أبي جمرة): Commentary on the verse requires explaining God’s majesty, worship, its forms and performance, the worshipper’s qualities, and the nature and manner of seeking aid. ALUSI (author): Only God may rightly receive worship, in law and reason, because He grants the greatest blessings, beginning with life and existence and all that follows from them. ALUSI (author): Worship can mean obedience, as in the command not to worship Satan. ELMALILI (author): The imagined worshipper pledges freedom from all but God, obedience to His commands, moral effort, and even sacrifice of life and worlds in God's path. IBNASHUR (الرازي): Al-Razi’s explanation of worship in 51:56 encompasses compliance with the whole body of religious law. IBNASHUR (ابن سينا): Ibn Sina explains that human interdependence requires exchange, justice, and a divinely prescribed law; a lawgiver and just recompense require knowledge of God, preserved by repeated worship. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The worship clause represents the Qur'an's commands and prohibitions; the path clause represents promise and warning. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): A third explanation of Umm al-Qur'an is that it contains the Qur'an's theoretical wisdom and practical rulings, including theology, prophecy, admonition, worship, transactions, morals, and law. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Worship trains individual and social perfection: it recalls God and recompense, disciplines the self, sustains just relations, and keeps thought on the Creator; this explains the purpose of creation stated in 51:56. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT (author): Leaving the object of seeking aid unstated makes the request cover every worldly and otherworldly need, not only worship or obedience. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT (author): The ordering parallels the command to worship God and then rely on Him. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT (الرازي): The servant’s deeds require worship and recognition that he cannot perform it without God’s aid."}, {"id": "1:5/q07/p2", "position": "Worship encompasses devoted action owed to God.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL (author): As the servant ceases serving rulers and relying on them for wealth or rank, he turns instead to worshipping God and seeking guidance and knowledge from Him.
